text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London fell sharply on heavy fund long liquidation. March lost $103 to close at $1,560 per tonne, while May gave up $123 to close at $1,540 per tonne. Some funds were seen rolling the heavy May positions further forward into July and September. The May/July spread stood at $20 over against $7 under on Friday.

Arabica futures in New York continued their correction with technical factors playing a prominent part. Fund oriented selling was at the forefront with little fresh fundamental news to offset the technical pressure. A lessening perception of near term supply tightness has clearly altered market sentiment for the short term, traders said.

Brazil's recent announcement of a higher than expected April coffee auction, and the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' technical group recommending an extra 500,000 bags to be released in January/June have contributed to the weaker trend. However, the weaker tone cannot disguise the fact that supplies remain tight. Moreover, Colombian truckers voted over the weekend to go out on strike on April 20, but the country's transport minister recently warned he would seek to outlaw the planned work stoppage. May lost 2.85 cents/lb to close at 162.90 cents/lb, while July gave up 1.75 cents/lb to close at 153.80 cents/lb. Traders said the long term view remains bullish and that coffee still has enormous upside potential.

COLOMBIA - The Colombian transport minister threatened to outlaw a strike by Colombian truck drivers scheduled for April 20. At a recent meeting, the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association (ACC), which represents about 80 per cent of the nation's truckers, voted to strike in protest at transport companies' failure to fulfil the terms of a deal signed at the end of a crippling 11-day stoppage in October. The accord hammered out to end the truckers October strike was backed by the government and included provisions for an increase in freight rates, downtime payments to truckers while they waited to on- and off-load cargoes and a revision of vehicle licensing fees and highway tolls. But ACC National Directorate member Maurio Quiroga said none of the terms of that agreement have been fulfilled and said truckers were still being forced to operate at a loss.

JAPAN - Japan imported 466,800 bags of coffee in January 1997, 29 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Brazil (103,800 vs 61,300 bags) and Colombia (106,800 vs 93,400 bags). The country imported 5.619 mn bags of coffee in 1996, 5.5 per cent more than was imported in 1995.

TAIWAN - Taiwan imported 193,600 bags of coffee in 1996. The country imports most of its coffee in the form of solubles. The two main suppliers in 1996 were South Korea (41,800 bags) and Singapore (21,400 bags). However, the country not only imports but also exports soluble coffee. The main country of destination in 1996 was the United States with 35,300 bags.
